Row.Text: Conversation steadily slows over the state dinner - someone is scraping their utensils along a plate: the American envoy. Dignitaries shudder at the sound, only to gasp when he asks for extra sauce. And the final insult: the American asks in a loud voice, “when are we gonna finally sign this thing?” Americans are bold, brash, but they have much to learn about diplomacy.
But this boldness is their strength. They break the cage of pompous pretension.
Is it possible to find envoys who know how to eat properly?

Still and silent, the stone-flanked, snow-crowned tirakuna watch over their valleys. In their shadows, the Inca build their first stone cities, balancing the gifts of the mountains: water, stones and light.
But cities can rise upon peaks as well: make the mountains kin. Learn to live in the heights.
The heights are beautiful, but the lowlands offer comfort.

From Kintu, all beings on earth come, and foremost of these are the Baganda. The ebika divide the Ganda people into clans, each clan with its own role. But what role do clans have when the Baganda become a nascent empire, when hunters and farmers must be clerks and potters?
The ebika still watch over the Baganda, and still frame Ganda life.
If time demands the clans change, then they change.

A debate between two French sages devolves into a duel. One maintains that man emerges as an entirely blank slate, and must learn reason. The other maintains that his opponent has been sleeping with his wife.
Debate – if not discretion – is the soul of France. Leave time for it.
Surely there must be some order!

Philosophers, scientists and holy men - rasool - are often one and the same: to discover the workings of the world below is to discover the mind of the world above. But what, one wonders, is the ultimate goal?
Spreading the truth to all that will hear.

The young raja-to-be sits on the water’s edge, twisting bamboo leaves into complicated shapes. Forms emerge: a tiny hull, a sliver of stalk for a mast, then great green sails. He sets it upon the water. Quickly, sails catch the faint breeze, and the ship is off – cutting the water’s still surface like a blade.
It is a portent. Look to the sea.
It is a hobby. He will soon learn statecraft.

Just as Maui pulls the islands from the sea, the wanderer Pa’ao lays down the customs that will govern Hawaii, the laws of kapu. Kapu preserves and regulates mana, allows it to flourish, and allows the Hawaiian people and their lands to prosper.
Set down kapu, render it into law, though it might limit some and embolden others.
With the bounty of the sea and land, Hawaiians will make their own way, unburdened by laws.

The taste of cloves and nutmeg. The rustle and snap of silk cloth. The red spit of betel. The gleam of gold. This is the fire of royalty, but it is a fire that needs constant feeding if it is to shine bright. The Majapahit need luxury to shine, and divinity needs separation.
The nobility are the heart of Majapahit. Let them shine.
The population is the heart of the Majapahit. Let them grow.

The Ming court lies behind walls, and walls, and walls. Some are of stone, some are of law, some are of custom and propriety. Critics say that Ming looks inward; supporters say there is nothing worth seeing anywhere else.
Behind these walls the shining sun and moon grow ever brighter.
Now is not the time for introspection.
The Troublesome Youths of the Steppe

Of all the troubles that plague empires, one of the most commonly experienced, but least talked-about, is sheep theft. The Mongol clans cannot stop raiding their neighbors, and the rivalries this creates are a constant nuisance in Mongol courts.
A strong sense of military discipline will rein them in.
Family heads and clan courts will solve these issues.

A young Norman piles stones on a hilltop. Wherever they are, the Normans are foreigners to that land. But here, she wonders, one might make a landscape that the Normans could call home. Certainly those living there might object, but in time…
Claim this land as Norman land via law and custom.
The Normans are, and will always be, a people apart from the land, ruling by steel and stone.

Water is unruly. Rivers flow without regard to borders; the flood tears away even the most carefully-laid foundations. But water is also potential: its flow bears goods to distant lands; its floods nurture the crops. So it is with the Songhai – they are difficult to bind, and go where they will.
A focus on the benefits of trade and production will incentivize settlement.

The Spanish scout pauses at the crest of a hill: here, the horizon stretches out. In the murky distance, there are shapes made both by river and ridge, but also by ambition and wanderlust. There are always those that see the beauty of the land…and seek to claim it.
An office, a department of exploration, expansion, and control – this is what Spain needs.
A knight’s valor, a raised banner, a desire for conquest - this is what Spain needs.

Meiji dawns upon the world, its citizens eagerly seeking the knowledge of others… and to use that knowledge to fuel its ever-growing furnaces. Meiji diplomats wander the wilderness, compiling notes on customs, discoveries, practices, and send their findings back to the central palace for processing. The dawn burns ever hotter.

Mexicans are those whose ancestors came from everywhere: some from across the seas, others over the mountain ridges, and still others from the next river valley over. Where they come together, then, is in the city square. And when they come together, they talk politics. Heatedly.
Revolution is inevitable. But it does not have to be catastrophic. Give time to consider how Mexico progresses.
Revolution is inevitable. But Mexico does not have to go into it alone. Give time for diplomacy.

A woman carrying two heavy buckets of water pauses in the shadow of a Mughal dome. The late afternoon sun turns the white marble to gold, and the first evening breeze cools the sweat on her skin. From inside the palace, the sound of laughter and a spike-fiddle extend to the street. She lifts her burden: in the shadow of Mughal luxury, Mughal subjects toil.
Beauty is a thing which is lost with familiarity. Preserve the barriers of ruler and ruled, wealthy and commonplace.
The Mughal rulers and their subjects will become one, over time.

Borders are not inscribed on the land. But one knows immediately when one rides into Prussian lands: the fields are plowed in straight lines; the ox-cart wheels shine with oil. And festivals are a relatively dull affair.
Pleasure gives way to production. Moderation will give way to prosperity.

The Manchu patrol receives guarded looks from local commoners as it watches its dominion – a parade of furs, flags, and bright metal. The Manchu Qing are a minority in these lands, but their military power and tight-knit clan groups make them formidable.
The Banner system can be opened to outsiders, given reform.
Qing rule is and will always be a machine for generating Manchu wealth.

In the light of two fires, two stories. In the smoky serfs’ hut, a grandmother tells the story of Vasilisa the Beautiful and Baba Yaga, of the iron teeth. Of wolves of iron and houses with chicken feet. Far away, in the capital, flambeaus illuminate a carefully-staged foreign theater production, with each set more elaborate than the last. Both audiences attend to their stories, eyes wide with imagination. Two Russias, in love with beauty.
The Russian nobility must appreciate their Slavic roots. What sets them apart, makes them Russian.
The Russian nobility will be international; the serfs can tell their wolf-stories.

Each Siamese city, each meuang, has its lord – one both in the physical world and one in the supernatural realm. Each subject pays their respect to their superior, on up the chain. But, for the court astrologer of {1_Capital}, this is not enough – all eyes should look to the rulers and divinities of the center, not to the local palace.
Revise the feudal system – local lords will be from {1_Capital} families, local traditions will be subordinate to {2_Capital} traditions.
In the diversity of cities and towns, there is strength.

Dr Rizal’s guide leads him through the wide avenues of the {1_SUBJECT_CIVILIZATION_ADJ} capital and across the farmlands of the countryside. Many sights and sounds are familiar, but some are not, and it is the latter that piques the poet’s curiosity.
